correctness.rationale: For all primes p=1 modulo 3, an order-three character and its orthogonality relation count each prescribed three-coset word. Six vectors with one nonzero exponent have complete sum zero; twelve with two nonzero exponents contribute at most sqrt(p) apiece; eight with three contribute at most 2sqrt(p) apiece by the classical Weil bound on polynomials with distinct linear roots. Omitting zero arguments contributes at most 24 overall; hence 27N >= p-28sqrt(p)-27 >0 for p>=900. Independently, verify.py exhaustively sieves the 74 eligible primes below 900, enumerates all p-3 positions, and compares full discrete-log and cubic-coset constructions. It finds exactly thirteen exceptional primes, with 283 missing only the all-cubes word. Therefore the sharp iff p>=307 theorem holds without extrapolating from finite data.

originality.rationale: Full-text comparison separates the established single-word theorem (Lehmer et al., 1962) from the all-27-word claim; 151 and 163 witness the nonimplication. Rabung and Jordan (1970) require all entries to lie in one class; Dietzel (2013) covers pairs; Hu and Chen (2020) treat reciprocal shifts. Searches of mathematical research records for cubic coset triples, 27 ternary words, and the claimed 307 threshold found no matching statement. The highly relevant but unavailable Emma Lehmer (1983) study remains a named residual risk: novelty is not certified by a failed search.

value.rationale: The simultaneous occurrence of every one of 27 local words is a natural complete support invariant for the order-three multiplicative coset partition. The sharp universal threshold and thirteen-prime exception list capture mixed-character obstructions, specifically at 151 and 163, that the established triple-of-cubic-residues theorem cannot see. This is not just a renaming or an elementary special case of that prior theorem: the full 27-word statement has strictly stronger logical content and a distinct combinatorial obstruction.
